newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia acts to keep solar race, Swiss in second.
newsitem.headline: Australia acts to keep solar race, Swiss in second.

text.p: The South Australian state government said on Thursday it had bought the rights to the World Solar Challenge car race, as a team of Swiss high school graduates breezed to second place in triennial event.

The government said it had paid founder Hans Tholstrup A$300,000 (US$237,000) for the rights to the race, which is run from Darwin in the north to Adelaide in the south. Tholstrup had indicated he wanted to bow out and there had been speculation that international bidders were looking to take it overseas.
The announcement came as the Swiss SCHooler Spirit '96 vechile crossed the finish line in a total running time of exactly 35 hours and an average speed of 86 kmph (53.44 mph).

On Wednesday, the solar-powered Japanese Honda Dream vehicle won the 1996 race, completing the 3,010 kms (1,870 miles) within four days in a running time of 33 hours and 32 minutes and an average speed of 89.76 kmph (55.77 mph).
Because the vechiles are solar powered they can operate only in daylight. While the Swiss team's running time was only 1-1/2 hours longer than that of the Japanse they finished a day later.
In third place was the Japanese Aisol III, in 37 hours and 18 minutes, averaging 80.7 kmph (50.14 mph).
About 40 the 57 starters still were on the road and most were expected over the weekend. The race ends on Monday whether or not all of the vehicles have finished.

SCHooler manager Marco Castagna, 21, told Reuters his 21-member team from Biel, 30 km (19 miles) north of the Swiss capital of Bern, was happy with its second place finish as it had beaten the time and speed of the 1993 winner.

The vehicle's body and solar panel were donated by former Biel University competitors, he said, and the team had spent just A$450,000 on the out-of-school project, a budget entry compared to the estimated A$10 million cost of the Honda car.

"We made improvements to the electronics and mechanics of the car. But our biggest and most time consuming problem was raising money for the project, and we only got our first sponsor days before the deadline for entering the race," Castagna said.
The race, founded in 1987, drew drew 57 solar powered cars and bicycles this year valued at about A$60 million,
The South Australian government said it would try to hold the race every two years, and that Tholstrup would continue as a technical adviser for five years with an option to continue.
